newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - EMU convergence trades not dead yet.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - EMU convergence trades not dead yet.

text.p: Recurring doubts about European high-yielders' ability to make the EMU grade have blown the froth off Italian and Spanish bond markets in recent days and sounded warning bells for convergence trades.

But falling inflation in peripheral Europe, continued sluggish economic growth and a soft mark mean BTP/Bund spreads may yet fall to around 140 basis points in the months ahead before bouncing back up, economists said.

"All we've really seen is that the market was ripe for a correction, investors have taken the opportunity to cash in on profits," said Bank Julius Bear economist Adrian Owens in London. "Nothing has changed fundamentally."
The hiccup in convergence trades was sparked by renewed fears of a delay to the timetable for a single European currency, compounded by vocal German opposition to a soft euro.
"The convergence factor has had a jolt, but the core situation is still good," said PaineWebber international economist Alison Cottrell.

"We still have low core interest rates and we still have some improvement in domestic inflation rates to come, particularly in Spain and also in Italy...That should be enough to mean these markets have a little bit left in them yet."
Cottrell expects the 10-year BTP/Bund spread to dip below 150 basis points within the next three months. She sees the Bono/Bund spread falling to below 100 or 90 basis points.
Italian and Spanish bonds have given up some ground to Bunds this week but the correction to date has been mild, with spreads still narrower than the levels of even four months ago.
By 1250 GMT on Tuesday, the BTP/Bund spread was at 157 basis points, up from 141 bps last Wednesday and the Bono/Bund gap was at 106 bps, up from 94 bps last week.
Julius Bear's Owens was even more optimistic about the amount of value left in convergence trades.
"At these levels, Italy represents a good buying opportunity," he said. "The fundamental information is quite positive, it's the comments from officials that hit the market."
Owens sees the BTP/Bund spread troughing at 130 basis points around spring with the Bono/Bund spread falling to 80 bps.

"There are a few more supportive factors still -- I think we've got further interest rate cuts in Italy...and a supplementary budget so further fiscal tightening which will also provide support," he said.
But economists are by no means agreed on spread direction.
David Brown, chief international economist at Bear Stearns in London, said investors had become over-optimistic about convergence trades and were due a shake-out.
"As people peel back their over-optimism, the risk is that we could see the 10-year spread widening to 350 basis points over the next six months," he said.
"What we've seen this week is the thin end of the wedge."
Economists agreed convergence trades would not last beyond the first half of the year, as skittish investors started to lose their cool with the approach of the single currency.
Cottrell sees the BTP/Bund spread ballooning to 175-180 basis points by August/September or even 200, depending on how much inter-European squabbling there is in the run-up to EMU.
Owens said the catalyst for a sustained widening of spreads would not come from comments by politicians or central bankers.
"When convergence comes to an end, there will need to be some other form of catalyst -- a hike in U.S interest rates, a dollar reversal, or rapid growth in Europe," he said.
Once that happens, investors will seek solace in British gilts or U.S. Treasuries in search of lower-risk yield.
"The UK is a convergence play in the second half," said Cottrell. "If (the opposition) Labour Party gets in, we'll get ERM speculation which will support the currency and help gilts."
On the other side of the Atlantic, U.S. Treasuries will lure disillusioned investors, Brown said. "People have been spoilt by high yielders for too long. 1997 will be the year of caution."
